title: Will and be going to
subtitle: I'll pick him up / I'm going to collect the children
summary: Choose between will and be going to for predictions, decisions, arrangements and if-sentences.

lesson.heading: Often either will do
lesson.text: For something that is planned, or that we think is likely to happen, either **will** or **be going to** is usually possible. In informal contexts we often prefer be going to.

examples.text: We **will study** climate change in a later part of the course.
examples.note: or We are going to study ...
or Where are you going to stay ...?

examples.text: The south of the city **won't be** affected by the power cuts.
examples.note: or ... isn't going to be affected ...

left.label: will - based on your opinion or experience
examples: Why not come over at the weekend? The children **will enjoy** seeing you again.
*A:* Shall I ask Lamar? *B:* No, she **won't want** to be disturbed.

right.label: be going to - based on present evidence
examples: The sky's gone really dark. There**'s going to be** a storm.
*A:* What's the matter with her? *B:* It looks like she**'s going to faint**.

lesson.heading: I bet, I expect, I imagine, I'm sure ...
lesson.text: To predict the future we often use **will** with *I bet, I expect, I hope, I imagine, I reckon, I think, I wonder* and *I'm sure*, and in questions with *think* and *reckon*.

examples.text: I imagine the stadium **will be** full for the match on Saturday.
That cheese smells awful. I bet nobody **will eat** it.
When do you think you**'ll finish** work?
Do you reckon he**'ll say** yes?

lesson.note: Be going to also works with these phrases, particularly in informal contexts.

left.label: will - decided as you speak
examples: I**'ll pick** him up at eight. (an offer; making an arrangement now)
*A:* Pineapples are on special offer this week. *B:* In that case, I**'ll buy** two.

right.label: be going to - decided before now
examples: I**'m going to collect** the children at eight. (this was previously arranged)
When I've saved up enough money, I**'m going to buy** a smartphone.

lesson.heading: Formal, detailed arrangements
lesson.text: In a formal style we use **will** rather than be going to for future events that have already been arranged in some detail.

examples.text: **Are** you **going to talk** at the meeting tonight?
The meeting **will begin** at 9 am. Refreshments **will be** available from 8:30 onwards.
examples.note: formal announcement of a detailed arrangement

lesson.heading: In if-sentences
lesson.text: When something - often something negative - is conditional on something else, either form works. But if the main clause does *not* depend on the if-clause, we use be going to. We use will for offers, requests, promises, ability, and logical consequences.

examples.text: You**'ll** / You**'re going to knock** that glass over if you're not careful.
I**'m going to open** a bottle of lemonade, if you want some.
examples.note: = I'm going to open it anyway. Do you want some?

examples.text: I**'ll open** a bottle of lemonade if you want some.
examples.note: = If you say you want some, I'll open it.

examples.text: If Erik phones, I**'ll let** you know.
If you look to your left, you**'ll see** the lake.
If you don't switch on the monitor first, the computer **won't come** on.

lesson.text: Ask what your prediction rests on: something you can see right now points to be going to; your own experience or judgement points to will.

exercises.prompt: Have you seen Nadia recently? She ___ another baby.
exercises.explanation: A prediction based on present evidence - you can see it - so be going to.

exercises.statement: The method is quite simple, and I'm sure it will be familiar to most of you already.
exercises.explanation: Correct. A prediction based on your own opinion or experience, and I'm sure goes naturally with will.

exercises.statement: Are these new skis yours? Will you take up skiing?
exercises.explanation: Are you going to take up skiing? The new skis are present evidence, so be going to.

exercises.prompt: Jamie says he ___ a politician when he grows up - and he's only five years old!
exercises.explanation: Jamie has already made his decision, so be going to.

exercises.statement: I hear you'll sell your car. How much do you want for it?
exercises.explanation: I hear you're going to sell your car. Selling it is a decision already made.

exercises.prompt: Match each question with the reply.

pairs.right: *B:* She says she's going to be sick.
*B:* I'm going to build a wall at the side of the garden.

pairs.left: *A:* Shall I give Ian another ring?
pairs.right: *B:* Yes, I expect he'll be home by now.

pairs.left: *A:* Did you get the theatre tickets?
pairs.right: *B:* No, I forgot all about them. I'll book them tomorrow.

pairs.left: *A:* When will you tell your boss you're leaving?
pairs.right: *B:* I'm not sure. Perhaps I'll try to see him later today.

exercises.prompt: If you want to help us, we ___ these trees at the bottom of the garden.
exercises.explanation: The planting does not depend on the if-clause - it is happening anyway - so be going to.

exercises.prompt: If I give you the money, ___ me some oranges when you're out?
exercises.explanation: Requests take will, not be going to.

exercises.prompt: If you listen carefully, you ___ an owl in the trees over there.
exercises.explanation: This is about ability - you'll be able to hear it - so will.

exercises.prompt: Announce formally, in a programme note, when the meeting starts and when refreshments are available.
exercises.answer: The meeting will begin at 9 am. Refreshments will be available from 8:30 onwards.
exercises.explanation: In a formal style, arrangements settled in detail take will.

exercises.prompt: He's been told that if he's late once more he ___.
exercises.explanation: Something negative conditional on something else: either will or be going to.

exercises.prompt: Which form does each sentence need? (... marks the gap.)

items.text: Why not come over at the weekend? The children ... enjoy seeing you again.
The sky's gone really dark. There ... be a storm.
*A:* Pineapples are on special offer this week. *B:* In that case, I ... buy two.
When I've saved up enough money, I ... buy a smartphone.
